This is a weekly series posted every Tuesday to discuss the terms anime fans use today.

Today's word is Deconstruction!

Context

Taken from Merriam-Webster:

the analytic examination of something (as a theory) often in order to reveal its inadequacy

Questions

  • Is this term overused?

  • What is the purpose of a deconstruction?

  • What are some series you find are actual deconstructions?
[Discussion] Anime Lexicon - Deconstruction | What is a deconstruction? (07.21.2015)

Alright, first, let's just get the direct questions out of the way:

Is the term overused?

Well, duh. I think this is because people tend to misidentify what a deconstruction is. A lot of what people call "deconstruction" is usually just "subversion," it's complicated because deconstructions very often make use of subverted tropes (almost by necessity) but a lot of subversions do not inherently make a deconstruction. Let's start off by defining the difference:

A subversion is when a show makes you think some sort of trope is going to happen, and then doesn't do it. For example, take the classic "boob-grope MC fall," wherein a harem MC trips into one of the heroines and inexplicably manages to end up with his knee in her crotch and his hands on her boobs. Then, per the cliche, he squeezes, wondering "What is this squishy thing in my hand?" Now, let's assume we're watching a show and the MC trips into a heroine and ends up grabbing something squishy:

  • If he's groping her boob in the standard harem-trip pose, it's played straight
  • If he's explicitly not groping her boob, instead cutting away to him with his hands in a bag of pudding or something, it's subverted.

A subversion, then, is when the show sets up a situation knowing your expectations and then does something different.

Now, here's the key: a subversion of a trope is the opposite of playing it straight. A deconstruction of a trope is playing it straighter than straight.

Going back to our grope-pose example: if the subversion is "MC actually misses entirely," the deconstruction would be "MC gropes the heroine, he's arrested for sexual harassment." On that, let's go to the next question:

What is the purpose of a deconstruction?

The function of a deconstruction is to explore a trope or narrative device to its logical end. Or, in other words, "What would happen if you tried this in reality?" What would happen, as Evangelion explores, if you threw an untrained highschooler into a mech and told him to save the world? What would happen, as Shinsekai Yori explores, if everyone got psychic powers?

At its simplest, deconstruction is a show taking that voice in the back of your head of "That would never work in real life" and incorporating that into the story itself. The hero who tries to take justice into his own hands as a vigilante ends up making things worse or becomes something even worse than the evil he was fighting in the first place (Watchmen); the harem MC who charms every girl around him ends up leaving them with broken hearts and emotional instability (School Days); living with a dozen monstergirls is actually a stressful and chaotic feat of logistics, both from a "Jesus Christ our food bill" standpoint to a "Sexytimes with a slimegirl will literally drown me" standpoint (Monster Musume).

So, what's the point? Why bother deconstructing a work of fiction?

Well, it's a simple part of a trope's development. It's like writing - you will never get something perfect on the first try. You have to break down an idea to its roots to look at what works and what doesn't work - why does a certain idea have appeal? What detracts from that appeal? What deserves more attention in this idea? You have to deconstruct a trope and show where it falls short in order to reconstruct it.

Series where I found deconstructions

  • Evangelion. Perhaps the easiest-to-name deconstruction of all time; wherein a lot of the themes of mecha anime are torn apart. Kids saving the world? Emotional wrecks. Hot-blooded pilots? Turns out that's a really bad tactic and psychologically damaging. Mecha linked to the brain of the pilot? Turns out that can be really fucking terrifying. There's too much to list that Eva deconstructs.
  • Tengen Toppa Gurren Lagann. Notable because it deconstructs, then reconstructs, its themes; for instance, being a happy-go-lucky yet suicidally stupid hero , but a the same time just because that's likely to happen doesn't mean you can't be one It also decon/recons the entire mecha genre - at first, it deconstructs via parody, by taking general conventions of mecha (let's combine! screaming-pilot superpowers!) and playing them to the point of being stupid, but then it reconstructs by turning things around and saying "Yeah, it's stupid, but it's also awesome." TTGL is a good example of how decon/recon doesn't necessarily need to infer a philosophical insight, it's an exploration of storytelling devices.
  • Madoka Magika is pretty obvious. Magical girls fighting evil? plus a brutal exploration of just how horrifying the mechanics behind being a magical girl might be (how do your powers work? why do you have them in the first place?).
  • Steins;Gate, twofold. First, Second,
  • Attack on Titan - of heroic sacrifices. Everyone who tries to die heroically either shows how people don't die heroically - they die sobbing and begging for their lives - or how "sacrifices" are done selfishly so that you can leave the fight while being remembered fondly, when in fact the harder (and more helpful) thing to do is to survive and keep fighting. Also explores the "So you turn into a hyperpowerful monster" idea, taking it to the "Yeah, everyone would think you're a freak who needs to be killed, not utilized."

Note that not all shows are "deconstructions" - not entirely. Shows that one would call "a deconstruction" are shows that either deconstruct their fundamental premises or genre - as is the case with Eva - or otherwise they contain elements of deconstruction - as is the case with, say, Unlimited Blade Works.

Here are some other shows that include partial deconstruction, but I'm running out of characters to elaborate with:

  • Kantai Collection (the anime). Y'know how you're sending these girls into combat? Do you think combat is fun???
  • Inou-Battle. Would normal kids actually run out and start fighting crime if they got powers, and randomized ones at that?
  • Fate/Stay. Archer's entire life
  • Oregairu. The snarky, over-intelligent loner archetype would, in reality, be perceived as an asshole. Also a lot of the standard anime romance themes. Reconstructs them in Season 2.
